domain_name: Quality of the Internal Audit Function

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. A risk manager runs the self-assessment
questions.question: The chief audit executive of a bank's three-person function asks the risk manager, a former internal auditor who knows the Standards well, to run the periodic self-assessment. Which view of this is most accurate?

options.A: Acceptable, and it also meets the external assessment requirement.
options.B: Not acceptable: self-assessment is for internal audit staff.
options.C: Acceptable as an internal assessment, not as an external one.
options.D: Acceptable, provided an outside assessor validates the results.

questions.key_concept: Periodic self-assessments may be done by people elsewhere in the organization who know internal audit practice; they never count as independent external assessments.
questions.pre_read: Recall who Standard 12.1 allows to perform internal assessments, and whom Standard 8.4 treats as independent.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.1 lets internal assessments be performed by the function itself or by others in the organization who know internal audit practice well enough, so a risk manager who was an internal auditor qualifies. Standard 8.4's considerations treat anyone from another department as not independent, so the work cannot stand in for the external assessment. Option D borrows independent validation, which belongs to the external route, not to internal assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Someone from another department sits outside internal audit but inside the organization, so the work cannot count as an independent external assessment.
wrong_explanations.B: Standard 12.1 lets people elsewhere in the organization who know internal audit practice well enough perform internal assessments.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: independent validation is how a self-assessment can meet the external requirement; an internal assessment needs no outside validation to be acceptable.

tips: Eliminate: A, because another department is never independent enough for an external assessment, and B, because Standard 12.1 allows knowledgeable people from elsewhere in the organization.
Final two: C beats D because independent validation belongs to the external route; an internal assessment by a knowledgeable insider needs none.
Exam cue: on CIA quality questions, sort the assessor first: inside the organization means internal assessment, whatever the department.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. An assessor whose designation lapsed
questions.question: A rail operator's chief audit executive proposes an independent firm's external assessment team: a lead whose Certified Internal Auditor designation has lapsed, an accountant and an IT specialist. Which change is most needed?

options.A: Include someone whose Certified Internal Auditor designation is active.
options.B: Add a member with experience as a chief audit executive.
options.C: Replace the accountant and the IT specialist with active designation holders.
options.D: Swap the IT specialist for an auditor from the parent company.

questions.key_concept: The external assessment team needs at least one member holding an active Certified Internal Auditor designation; other qualifications are considerations.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 8.4 requires of the assessment team's qualifications, and what it only suggests weighing.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.4 requires the chief audit executive, in choosing the assessor or team, to make sure one or more of its people hold an active Certified Internal Auditor designation. A lapsed designation does not count, so the team falls short until someone with an active one is on it. Experience as a chief audit executive is among the qualifications the considerations suggest, useful but not required, so option B ranks below the requirement.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: senior internal audit leadership is a qualification the considerations suggest weighing; the requirement still unmet is an active Certified Internal Auditor.
wrong_explanations.C: One active Certified Internal Auditor on the team is the requirement; swapping out the accountant and IT specialist would also lose skills the review needs.
wrong_explanations.D: An auditor from a parent company comes from a related organization and is not considered independent for an external assessment.

tips: Eliminate: C, because one active designation holder meets the requirement and other skills add value, and D, because people from a parent company are not independent for this purpose.
Final two: A beats B because an active Certified Internal Auditor is a requirement, while chief audit executive experience is a suggested qualification.
Exam cue: on CIA external assessment questions, check the one firm qualification first: at least one active Certified Internal Auditor.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. Reporting a self-assessment's results
questions.question: A periodic self-assessment at a copper miner finds two nonconformances with the Standards. What is most clearly required in the chief audit executive's report to the board and senior management?

options.A: The results, once both nonconformances have been put right.
options.B: The results, with an independent assessor's validation of them.
options.C: The results, with senior management's approval of the fixes.
options.D: The results, with action plans and their proposed timelines.

questions.key_concept: Periodic self-assessment results go to the board and senior management with action plans and a proposed timeline for the nonconformances found.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.1 requires the chief audit executive to do with the results of periodic self-assessments.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.1 requires the chief audit executive to build action plans, with a proposed timeline, for the nonconformances and improvement chances a periodic self-assessment finds, and to communicate the results and the plans to the board and senior management. Waiting until both are fixed, option A, delays what the board needs to oversee quality and skips the plan it is meant to agree. Validation and senior management approval are not part of this step.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: fixing the gaps is the aim, but the results and dated action plans go to the board and senior management now, not after the repairs.
wrong_explanations.B: Independent validation is a route to meeting the external assessment requirement; internal assessment results are reported without it.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management gives input, but the report needs action plans with a timeline, and the considerations have actions agreed with the board.

tips: Eliminate: B, because independent validation belongs to the external assessment route, and C, because the report needs dated action plans, and actions are agreed with the board.
Final two: D beats A because results and dated action plans are reported now, so the board can oversee the fixes rather than hear of them afterward.
Exam cue: on CIA quality questions, a self-assessment's results travel with action plans and a timeline to the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. Topical Requirements in quality assessments
questions.question: Planning a port authority's periodic self-assessment, the chief audit executive (CAE) hears an audit manager say Topical Requirements are topic rules outside the quality program. Which reply by the CAE is most accurate?

options.A: Agreed: assessors judge conformance with the Standards, not topic rules.
options.B: Not so: quality assessments evaluate conformance with them as well.
options.C: Partly: the external assessment checks them, internal ones do not.
options.D: Not so: the board checks conformance with them each year.

questions.key_concept: Topical Requirements are mandatory for assurance work, and conformance with them is evaluated in quality assessments, internal and external.
questions.pre_read: Recall what a Topical Requirement says about documenting applicability and about quality assessments.
questions.correct_explanation: Each Topical Requirement makes conformance mandatory and says quality assessments will evaluate it, and it requires kept evidence that every requirement was assessed for applicability, with reasons for any exclusion. Standard 8.3's program covers every aspect of the function through internal and external assessments, so the planned self-assessment checks Topical Requirement conformance too. Option C limits that to the external assessment, which neither source does.

wrong_explanations.A: Topical Requirements are mandatory and used with the Standards; the requirement itself says quality assessments evaluate conformance with it.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the external assessor does check them, but the quality program covers every aspect of the function, internal assessments included.
wrong_explanations.D: The board considers quality results when it assesses the function, an essential condition; conformance itself is evaluated in the quality assessments, internal and external.

tips: Eliminate: A, because conformance with a Topical Requirement is mandatory for assurance work and assessed, and D, because the board reviews quality results as an essential condition, while quality assessments do the evaluating.
Final two: B beats C because quality assessments, internal ones included, evaluate Topical Requirement conformance; the program covers every aspect of the function.
Exam cue: on CIA quality questions, Topical Requirements sit inside the quality program; keep applicability records for the assessors.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Disclosing nonconformance with the Standards. What the record must contain
questions.question: An airport's board defers its external assessment past the five-year limit until an internal audit merger ends; the chief audit executive records the circumstance and reason. What else does the record most need?

options.A: The alternative actions taken and the impact of those actions.
options.B: A firm target date for completing the deferred external assessment.
options.C: A statement that the rest of the function conforms.
options.D: A statement from the planned assessor on current conformance.

questions.key_concept: A nonconformance record states four things: the circumstance, the alternative actions taken, their impact and the rationale.
questions.pre_read: Recall the four elements Standard 4.1 requires the chief audit executive to document and communicate when a requirement cannot be met.
questions.correct_explanation: When a requirement cannot be met, Standard 4.1 requires the chief audit executive to document and communicate the circumstance, the alternative actions taken, the impact of those actions and the rationale. The chief audit executive has recorded two of the four. A target date, option B, is sensible and fits the action plans Standard 12.1 asks for after self-assessments, but it is not one of the elements this disclosure must carry.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the external assessment plan will need a new date, but that plan is separate; Standard 4.1's record holds circumstance, alternative actions, impact and rationale.
wrong_explanations.C: Conformance elsewhere is expected, but a statement of it is not one of the four elements; the record still lacks the alternative actions and their impact.
wrong_explanations.D: No assessor has reviewed the function yet; a nonconformance record is the chief audit executive's own account, not an assessor's statement.

tips: Eliminate: C, because a statement about the rest of the function is not one of the four elements, and D, because the record is the chief audit executive's account, made before any assessor arrives.
Final two: A beats B because alternative actions and their impact are required elements, while a target date belongs to other action plans.
Exam cue: on CIA nonconformance questions, check for all four elements: circumstance, alternative actions, impact and rationale.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Disclosing nonconformance with the Standards. A law that blocks one requirement
questions.question: A state secrecy law bars a shipyard's internal auditors from keeping the engagement documentation the Standards require for naval contracts. Which approach by the chief audit executive is best?

options.A: Cite the secrecy law as a requirement used with the Standards.
options.B: Disclose the function's nonconformance with the Standards as a whole.
options.C: Conform with all other parts and disclose the part the law blocks.
options.D: Leave the matter for the external assessor to judge and report.

questions.key_concept: When a law prevents conformance with part of the Standards, the function conforms with every other part and discloses the part it cannot meet.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 4.1 requires when laws or regulations prohibit conformance with part of the Standards.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 4.1 requires that, when a law or regulation prohibits conformance with any part of the Standards, the function conform with all the other parts and make appropriate disclosures, with the chief audit executive documenting the circumstance, alternative actions, impact and rationale. Option A applies a different rule in 4.1: citing other authoritative requirements used alongside the Standards. A secrecy law that blocks a requirement is a nonconformance, not an added framework.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 4.1 does require citing other authoritative requirements used with the Standards, but a law blocking a requirement is a nonconformance that must be disclosed.
wrong_explanations.B: Only the blocked part is a nonconformance; Standard 4.1 requires conformance with every other part, so a blanket statement overstates the gap.
wrong_explanations.D: Disclosure is the chief audit executive's duty now; the external assessor later uses that record and never replaces it.

tips: Eliminate: B, because only the blocked part fails and the rest still binds, and D, because the chief audit executive discloses now rather than leaving it to an assessor.
Final two: C beats A because a law that stops conformance creates a nonconformance to disclose, while citing other requirements is for frameworks used alongside the Standards.
Exam cue: on CIA questions where a law blocks one requirement, conform with the rest and disclose the blocked part.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Disclosing nonconformance with the Standards. A gap that reaches the whole function
questions.question: A savings bank's self-assessment finds two years of internal audit plans rested on undocumented risk assessments, a gap in the function's overall operation. Which step is most clearly required of the chief audit executive?

options.A: Disclose it in the final communication of each later engagement.
options.B: Disclose it and its impact to the board and senior management.
options.C: Tell senior management, which decides whether the board hears it.
options.D: Document this year's assessment and treat the gap as closed.

questions.key_concept: A nonconformance affecting the whole function goes, with its impact, to the board and senior management; a one-engagement gap goes in its own final communication.
questions.pre_read: Recall where Standards 12.1 and 15.1 send a nonconformance, depending on whether it affects one engagement or the whole function.
questions.correct_explanation: Standards 12.1 and 8.3 require the chief audit executive to report internal assessment results, with action plans, to the board and senior management, and 12.1 adds that a nonconformance affecting the function's overall scope or operation goes to both with its impact. Two years of plans without the documented risk assessment Standard 9.4 requires is such a gap. Option A is Standard 15.1's route for one engagement's nonconformance.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: Standard 15.1 puts one engagement's nonconformance in its final communication; this gap sits in the plan behind every engagement, so both bodies hear it.
wrong_explanations.C: A function-wide nonconformance must go to both the board and senior management; senior management cannot filter what the board receives.
wrong_explanations.D: Documenting this year's assessment fixes the cause, but two years of plans rested on undocumented assessments; that nonconformance is still reported with its impact.

tips: Eliminate: C, because senior management cannot decide what the board hears about nonconformance, and D, because fixing the cause does not remove the duty to disclose.
Final two: B beats A because a gap in the plan reaches the whole function, so it goes to the board and senior management, not into engagement reports.
Exam cue: on CIA nonconformance questions, match the route to the reach: one engagement in its report, the whole function to the board and senior management.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Performance measures for internal audit. A scorecard with no targets
questions.question: An insurer's chief audit executive keeps a scorecard reporting plan completion, key-risk coverage and board satisfaction, each beside last year's figure; an analyst validates the figures' accuracy quarterly. What does the scorecard most lack?

options.A: A findings count per auditor to show productivity.
options.B: A periodic check that the reported figures are accurate.
options.C: Countable measures in place of board satisfaction.
options.D: A target for each measure, set against its objective.

questions.key_concept: Each performance objective needs targets, quantitative and qualitative; a measure with no target shows a trend but not success or shortfall.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.2's considerations say about targets, qualitative measures and checking the accuracy of reported measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.2's considerations say the chief audit executive should set quantitative and qualitative targets to track progress toward each performance objective, and should periodically validate the accuracy of reported measures. The scorecard's figures are checked quarterly, so accuracy is covered; what is missing is any level to judge them against. Beside last year's figure, a measure shows direction, not whether the objective is met.

wrong_explanations.A: Judging auditors by the number of findings can impair objectivity, as Standard 2.2's considerations warn; it adds volume, not a target.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: validating accuracy is a step the considerations suggest, but the stem says an analyst already validates the figures every quarter.
wrong_explanations.C: The considerations call for qualitative as well as quantitative targets; board satisfaction shows value that counts alone miss.

tips: Eliminate: A, because findings counts can harm objectivity, and C, because qualitative measures such as board satisfaction belong in a balanced set.
Final two: D beats B because the figures' accuracy is already validated each quarter; without targets they still cannot show whether objectives are met.
Exam cue: on CIA scorecard questions, every measure needs a target; a trend alone shows direction, not achievement.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Performance measures for internal audit. A falling action plan completion rate
questions.question: A hotel group's rate of action plans completed with the intended result fell from 80 to 55 percent; a director calls it internal audit's failure. Which reply by the chief audit executive is best?

options.A: Disagree: the rate measures management alone, not internal audit.
options.B: Agreed: the rate measures how well internal audit follows up.
options.C: Partly: it reflects management's follow-through as well as internal audit's.
options.D: Partly: a shared result, so internal audit helps finish the actions.

questions.key_concept: Action plan completion is a useful measure, but management completes actions, so the rate is not internal audit's performance alone.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.2's considerations say about measuring the share of action plans that achieve the desired outcome.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.2's considerations list the share of action plans management completes with the desired outcome as a measure internal audit may track, and note it is not only a reflection of internal audit's performance: management is responsible for completing the actions and achieving the outcomes. The chief audit executive should read the drop as a shared signal worth analyzing. Option D sees the shared result but has internal audit help finish actions management owns.

wrong_explanations.A: Management completes the actions, but the considerations call the rate not exclusively internal audit's performance, so it still says something about internal audit's work.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit tracks the rate and follows up, but management completes the actions, so the considerations do not treat the rate as internal audit's performance alone.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: the rate is a shared result, but completing actions stays with management; internal audit confirms implementation, and helping finish them would leave it assessing its own work.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the considerations do not treat the rate as management's alone, and B, because management completes the actions, so the rate is not internal audit's alone.
Final two: C beats D because management owns completing the actions; internal audit tracks and confirms them, and helping finish them would leave it assessing its own work.
Exam cue: on CIA performance questions, ask who controls the result a measure counts before calling it internal audit's performance.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Performance measures for internal audit. Savings beside a quality shortfall
questions.question: A port's internal audit function finished its plan 15% under budgeted hours, but quality reviews found a third of workpapers did not support conclusions. Which reading by the chief audit executive is best?

options.A: Efficient, but the workpaper gap is an issue needing an action plan.
options.B: Efficient; report the savings and keep the workpaper gap in-house.
options.C: Next year's budget can drop to the hours actually used.
options.D: Workpaper reviews are supervision tools, not performance measures.

questions.key_concept: Read performance measures together: an efficiency gain does not show good performance when quality falls, and a shortfall needs an action plan.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.2 requires once measures reveal an issue, and what Standards 8.3 and 12.1 count when judging quality.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.2 requires an action plan for issues the performance measures reveal, and Standards 12.1 and 8.3 require internal assessment results, ongoing monitoring included, to reach the board and senior management. Finishing under budget looks efficient, but workpapers that do not support conclusions undercut the results the board relies on. Option B keeps the gap in-house, reporting only the favorable measure.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the savings are real, but internal assessment results, ongoing monitoring included, must reach the board and senior management; keeping the gap in-house withholds them.
wrong_explanations.C: Cutting the budget to the hours used would lock in the conditions behind the weak workpapers before their cause is known.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 12.1's considerations name supervisory reviews of workpapers as a primary way to monitor conformance and performance, so their results are performance evidence.

tips: Eliminate: C, because cutting hours before finding the quality gap's cause could deepen it, and D, because quality reviews are part of monitoring the function's performance.
Final two: A beats B because a quality gap the measures reveal needs an action plan, and internal assessment results go to the board and senior management, not stay in-house.
Exam cue: on CIA measures questions, set speed or cost results beside quality results before calling the function's performance good.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. Self-assessments with no written record
questions.question: At a credit union, the chief audit executive's team rates conformance with every standard at a yearly workshop and keeps only the summary it reports. What is most needed before next year's external assessment?

options.A: An active Certified Internal Auditor among the raters at each workshop.
options.B: A full written record of each internal assessment and its results.
options.C: An outside assessor's validation of each yearly workshop.
options.D: Board minutes recording the discussion of each summary.

questions.key_concept: Internal assessments must be documented, because the external assessment evaluates them; a summary of results is not that record.
questions.pre_read: Recall what Standard 12.1 requires of internal assessments in relation to the external assessment.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.1 requires a documented record of every internal assessment, which the independent assessor then reviews as part of the external assessment. A summary reports results but does not show how each standard was rated or on what evidence, so the assessor has nothing to evaluate. Board minutes cannot fill that gap: they record that a summary was discussed, not how the assessment was done.

wrong_explanations.A: An active designation is required on the external assessment team; for periodic self-assessments the considerations list it as one option among experienced raters, not a requirement.
wrong_explanations.C: Independent validation is an optional route for meeting the external requirement through a self-assessment; yearly internal work needs documenting, not outside validation.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: minutes show the results were discussed, but Standard 12.1 asks for the internal assessment itself to be documented for the external assessor.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the active designation rule belongs to the external team, and C, because independent validation is an optional route to meet the external requirement.
Final two: B beats D because the external assessor evaluates the internal assessment itself; minutes show only that the board discussed a summary.
Exam cue: on CIA quality questions, internal and external assessments connect: the external assessor evaluates the documented internal ones.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. Dropping the periodic self-assessment
questions.question: Every workpaper at a life insurer is reviewed against a checklist, so the chief audit executive plans to stop the function's periodic self-assessment. Which view of the plan is most accurate?

options.A: Sound, if the board approves the change to the quality program.
options.B: Sound, if the checklist covers every standard, beyond engagement ones.
options.C: Unsound: an independent party must judge the function's conformance.
options.D: Unsound: a periodic assessment is still required beside ongoing monitoring.

questions.key_concept: Internal assessment needs ongoing monitoring and a periodic assessment by the function or knowledgeable insiders; strong supervision does not replace the periodic look.
questions.pre_read: Recall the parts Standard 12.1 requires in the methodology for internal assessments.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.1 requires the chief audit executive's internal assessment methodology to include both ongoing monitoring and periodic self-assessments, or assessments by others in the organization who know internal audit practice. Checklist review of workpapers is ongoing monitoring. Its considerations add that periodic self-assessments look at every standard and the function as a whole, but even a checklist covering every standard would not remove the requirement for the periodic layer.

wrong_explanations.A: The board cannot waive a requirement of the Standards; dropping a required part of internal assessment would be a nonconformance to disclose, not a change to approve.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: periodic self-assessments do reach beyond engagement standards, but Standard 12.1 requires them as a separate part of internal assessment, whatever the checklist covers.
wrong_explanations.C: Standard 12.1 lets the function and knowledgeable people elsewhere in the organization perform internal assessments; independence is required of external assessors.

tips: Eliminate: A, because no approval can waive a requirement of the Standards, and C, because internal assessments are done by the function or knowledgeable people in the organization.
Final two: D beats B because Standard 12.1 requires a periodic assessment as a separate part beside ongoing monitoring; a broader checklist does not merge the two.
Exam cue: on CIA quality-program questions, count the layers: ongoing monitoring, periodic self-assessment, then an external assessment at least every five years.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Performance measures for internal audit. Objectives drafted without stakeholder input
questions.question: A ferry operator's chief audit executive (CAE) drafts the function's performance objectives from the internal audit charter and strategy, consulting nobody outside the function, for the board's approval. Which change is most clearly required?

options.A: Have the board and senior management set the objectives, the CAE tracking.
options.B: Consider the board's and senior management's input and expectations.
options.C: Draw on the Principles as well as the charter and strategy.
options.D: Have senior management approve the objectives instead of the board.

questions.key_concept: The chief audit executive develops the performance objectives but must consider the board's and senior management's input and expectations in doing so.
questions.pre_read: Recall who Standard 12.2 says develops performance objectives, whose input must be considered, and who approves them.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 12.2 requires the chief audit executive to develop the function's performance objectives and, while doing so, to take account of what the board and senior management contribute and expect; here nobody was consulted. Drawing on the Principles as well as the charter and strategy is something its considerations say should be done: good practice, not the required change. The board's yearly approval is an essential condition for the board, and is already sought.

wrong_explanations.A: Standard 12.2 has the chief audit executive develop the objectives; senior management gives input and the board approves them under Standard 8.3's essential conditions, rather than either setting them.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: the considerations say objectives should reflect the Principles too, but that is a should; considering the board's and senior management's input is a must.
wrong_explanations.D: Standard 8.3 lists approving the performance objectives at least yearly for the board; senior management provides input on them.

tips: Eliminate: A, because the chief audit executive develops the objectives rather than the board and senior management, and D, because senior management gives input while the board approves.
Final two: B beats C because Standard 12.2 requires considering the board's and senior management's input; drawing on the Principles is a should in its considerations.
Exam cue: on CIA performance-objective questions, sort the roles: the chief audit executive develops, senior management gives input, the board approves.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. External assessments rotated among peers
questions.question: The chief audit executives of four banks plan external assessments in a cycle: each bank's conflict-free team, including an active Certified Internal Auditor, assesses the next bank in line. Which view is most accurate?

options.A: Acceptable: three or more peers in rotation may be independent.
options.B: Not acceptable: banks in one sector may count as related organizations.
options.C: Acceptable as self-assessments, but each needs independent validation.
options.D: Not acceptable: peer functions cannot assess each other independently.

questions.key_concept: Two organizations assessing each other are not independent; a rotation among three or more peers can be, with qualified, conflict-free assessors.
questions.pre_read: Recall how Standard 8.4's considerations treat reciprocal peer reviews, rotations among peers and related organizations.
questions.correct_explanation: Standard 8.4 requires a qualified, independent assessor or team with at least one active Certified Internal Auditor. Its considerations rule out two-way swaps but accept that a rotation among three or more peers may count as independent, with care over conflicts. Here no bank is assessed by the bank it assesses, and each team is qualified and conflict-free, so the rotation itself can be the external assessment; no separate validation is needed.

wrong_explanations.B: Related organizations are a parent, an affiliate in the same group or a body with oversight duties; separate banks in one sector are peers, not related organizations.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: self-assessment with independent validation is a separate route; a rotation among three or more peers can itself be the independent external assessment.
wrong_explanations.D: Among peer organizations, only reciprocal reviews between two are ruled out; Standard 8.4's considerations allow a rotation among three or more peers to count as independent.

tips: Eliminate: B, because related organizations are a parent, affiliate or overseer, not sector peers, and D, because only two-way swaps are ruled out.
Final two: A beats C because a rotation among three or more peers can itself be the independent external assessment; independent validation belongs to the self-assessment route.
Exam cue: on CIA external-assessment questions, count the parties: two reviewing each other is not independent; a rotation among three or more can be.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Quality assurance and improvement program. Third-party conformance in a self-assessment
questions.question: When the Third-Party Topical Requirement took effect, a hydropower company's chief audit executive added third-party checks to the periodic self-assessment. Which check is most clearly needed to judge conformance with the requirement?

options.A: Whether the internal audit plan records which engagements cover each requirement.
options.B: Whether management monitors each prioritized third party's performance against its contract.
options.C: Whether third-party assurance work retained applicability evidence and exclusion reasons.
options.D: Whether each advisory engagement on third parties conformed with the requirement.

questions.key_concept: A quality assessment judges Topical Requirement conformance from internal audit's kept evidence: each requirement assessed for applicability, a reason for each exclusion.
questions.pre_read: Separate what internal audit must keep from where it may choose to keep it, and from management's own duties.
questions.correct_explanation: The Third-Party Topical Requirement requires assurance work to conform, says quality assessments evaluate that conformance, and requires kept evidence that each requirement was assessed for applicability, with a reason for every exclusion. Under Standard 12.1, the chief audit executive's self-assessment looks for that evidence. Option A comes closest, but the user guide lets auditors record coverage in the plan or in the engagement workpapers, so a plan record is a choice, not the test.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the user guide lets auditors record coverage in the plan or in each engagement's workpapers, so a plan record is one option, not a requirement.
wrong_explanations.B: Management's monitoring of prioritized third parties is what a third-party assurance engagement assesses; a self-assessment judges whether internal audit conformed, not how management runs vendors.
wrong_explanations.D: A Topical Requirement binds assurance work; for advisory work, conforming is only recommended, so advisory conformance is not what judging conformance needs.

tips: Eliminate: B, because management's monitoring of third parties is what an assurance engagement assesses, not what a quality assessment judges, and D, because conformance is only recommended for advisory work.
Final two: C beats A because kept applicability evidence with exclusion reasons is required, while recording coverage in the plan rather than the workpapers is the auditors' choice.

Exam cue: on CIA quality questions about a Topical Requirement, the assessor checks internal audit's own evidence: each requirement assessed for applicability, each exclusion reasoned. Where it is filed is a may.
